newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria seeks Russian aid for reactors' upgrading.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria seeks Russian aid for reactors' upgrading.

text.p: Bulgaria and Russia have started talks on upgrading of Bulgaria's four 440-megawatt nuclear reactors at Kozloduy in a bid to operate them safely for as long as possible, the plant's chairman said on Thursday.
"We have started talks with Russia for implementing a complex upgrading programme and asked them to extend us a credit for it," Kiril Nikolov told a news conference.
He said preliminary estimates for the programme were $400 million, $100 million of which would go towards the construction of a storage facility for spent nuclear fuel.
"There is a tendency to pay the credit by exporting goods to Russia," Nikolov added.
The Soviet-made Kozloduy plant, which also has two more modern 1,000-megawatt reactors, produces more than 40 percent of Bulgaria's electricity.

The plant's two oldest reactors, number one and two, have long been at the centre of international concern over their safety and a mission of the International Atomic Energy Agency recommended their closure in 1991.
They were restarted in 1992 and 1993 respectively but were closed periodically for further repairs.
Kozloduy plans to complete the third and final stage of the safety reconstruction programme of its four reactors in 1997 and has already invested 2.2 billion levs in it.
In 1993 wealthy European countries through the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development donated 24 million Ecus for equipment for reactors three and four.
Nikolov said 16 million Ecus had been used to purchase basic equipment.
Reactor number one was switched off last May amid international concern over the safety of the metal of its vessel.
Nikolov said preliminary results from analysis of the metal's samples were positive.
"We expect the final results in the middle of December and can decide the reactors' restart in the middle of January," he said.
The analysis, carried out by the plant's Russian designer, the Korchatov institute, will be discussed with Bulgarian experts at a meeting in Sofia next week.
German firm Siemens AG is carrying out its own analysis and the Bulgarians will go to Germany in the first week of December to discuss their results, officials said.
Nikolov said the plant was prepared to supply up to 2,800 megawatts this winter, without reactor number one.

Kozloduy's most modern 1,000-megawatt reactor number six, which was switched off on Monday due to a minor incident with an air relief valve in its second steam generator, is expected to be repaired by next week.
